prompt: A hypothetical friend says: 'I buy shares today. I borrow money to buy more. I sell within an hour to catch the next move.' Which label fits best?

explanations.a: Investing means holding a business for years, with the return coming from earnings and growth. A one-hour time frame does not fit that.
explanations.b: Trading follows written rules and limits on each trade. The description gives no rules. Borrowing to buy more, with no stated limit, is the opposite of that.
explanations.d: A savings plan is a regular habit of setting money aside. Nothing in the description is saving.

prompt: A hypothetical plan risks Rs 3,000 to make Rs 500 per trade. Leave out costs. What win rate, in percent to one decimal place, do you need just to break even?
solution: Let W be the win rate. Break-even: W x 500 = (1 - W) x 3,000. So 500W = 3,000 - 3,000W, which gives 3,500W = 3,000. W = 3,000 / 3,500 = 6/7 = 0.857..., so 85.7%. Check: 6/7 x 500 = Rs 428.57 and 1/7 x 3,000 = Rs 428.57. They are equal. Common wrong answers: 50% (treats the two outcomes as equal), 14.3% (flips the ratio to 500 / 3,500), and 85% (rounded without working).

prompt: A friend says: 'A high win rate means I make money.' Is that right?

options.text: Yes. Frequent wins add up to profit.
No. Win rate only measures how often trades win. The size of wins and losses decides the result too.
Yes, as long as the trader never takes a loss.

explanations.a: Frequent wins do not add up to profit if each loss is bigger than each win. For example, a hypothetical plan that wins 60% of trades for Rs 500 and loses 40% of trades for Rs 3,000 averages 0.6 x 500 - 0.4 x 3,000 = 300 - 1,200 = minus Rs 900 per trade. Size matters. Later chapters cover position size.
explanations.c: Never taking a loss is not a plan. Every trade can lose money. This book treats that as the main problem.

prompt: Statement: 'The backtest made Rs 1 lakh, so it will earn the same live.' Which part of this statement is the mistake?

options.text: 'so it will earn the same live'

explanations.a: A backtest is a test of the past. Reporting what it made is fine if you label it as backtested. The first half is not the error.
explanations.c: Backtests are useful for testing an idea. The mistake is moving from a simulated result straight to a live expectation. Live trading adds costs, real order prices and real behaviour. The simulation does not have these.

prompt: A friend promises you steady monthly income from trading. Which response treats the claim correctly?

options.text: Steady monthly income is possible, so invest once you have seen the friend's returns.
The claim has no proof yet. Ask what record exists. Ask if it is theoretical, backtested or live. No one can promise steady income.
Ignore it, because only losses are worth studying.

explanations.a: No one can promise steady income, so the book does not treat this as possible. A friend's returns are not proof, unless there is a clear record and you know what type of record it is.
explanations.c: The claim deserves a question, not a dismissal. Asking for proof is part of learning to judge claims.

prompt: Which THREE of these are common ways an active trader loses money? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Costs: brokerage, taxes and other charges on every trade
Putting too much money into one trade
Holding a mix of companies for decades

explanations.b: A written per-trade limit is a loss control. It is the opposite of a loss path.
explanations.e: Holding many companies for a long time is an investing approach. It is not one of the three trading loss paths in this chapter.
